title: Painting quotes, variations and colour approval
audience: Painters who quote, manage variations and obtain colour approval from clients
learningOutcomes: Write a painting quote that states the scope, the surfaces, the system, the coats and the exclusions.
Manage variations in writing before they are performed.
Obtain written colour approval and state the effect of a colour change on the price.

instruction.heading: A quote states what is included and what is not
instruction.body: A painting quote is the document that sets the client's expectations for the job, and most painting disputes start where the quote was vague. It should name the property and the surfaces to be painted, room by room and elevation by elevation, so that the client can see what the price covers. It should state the preparation included, such as washing, filling, sanding and masking, and say whether the preparation is part of the price. It should name the paint system, meaning the primer, undercoat and topcoat, and the number of coats for each surface. It should state how colour is approved, the sheen level and the date the quote is valid until. Exclusions matter as much as inclusions. Repairs to damp, plaster defects, mould treatment, assessment of older surfaces for lead or asbestos, furniture moving and the repair of cladding or timber are commonly excluded, and each exclusion should be written out rather than implied. A quote that says the house will be painted is not enough. Give the client a list that shows exactly what the price covers and what it does not.

instruction.heading: Quotes, estimates and what the client can rely on
instruction.body: Consumer guidance in Victoria advises clients to compare written quotes for the same work, to confirm what each quote covers, and to watch for cheaper quotes that leave items out or use a base rate that does not cover the finish they want. It also advises asking how changes to the quote or the timeframe will be handled, and recording changes in writing and signed off before they are made (Consumer Victoria, getting quotes; last updated 20 October 2025). The Australian Consumer Law guarantee of due care and skill applies to services. Under it, the work should be of the standard a competent provider with average skill and experience would deliver, and the provider should take reasonable steps to avoid loss or damage (ACCC, consumer rights and guarantees). A quote therefore should describe the work that the business is able and willing to deliver to that standard, and should not promise results the paint cannot give, such as hiding a crack that is not repaired.

instruction.heading: Check the licence position before the quote is issued
instruction.body: The value of the work and the state where it is done decide whether a licence or registration is needed, and the check belongs before the quote is sent. New South Wales: you need a contractor licence to do any residential building or trade work, including painting, which is valued at more than $5,000 in labour and materials (including GST) (NSW Government painting work page, last updated 23 June 2026). Since 2015, stand-alone contracts for internal paintwork no longer need a licence, unless the paintwork is part of other home building work. Western Australia: painting work valued at $1,000 or more requires a licence, which is painting contractor registration (WA Government painters' scope of work page, last updated 23 December 2025). Victoria: painting-only jobs need no registration. You must register with the BPC if you are using a combination of skills, such as plastering and painting, to complete a job (Consumer Victoria registration page, last updated 9 July 2025). Queensland: the licence position for painting-only work is not confirmed by an official source. South Australia, Tasmania, the Australian Capital Territory and the Northern Territory: the licence position for painting is not confirmed by an official source. Each check should be recorded with the state, the value, the date and the page checked.

instruction.heading: Written contracts and variations
instruction.body: A variation is any change to the agreed scope. It includes extra coats, extra surfaces, a different system, a change of colour that needs more coats, and repairs that are found during preparation. In New South Wales, the government guidance for residential building contracts says that a variation must be in writing, attached to the contract, and signed by both the client and the contractor or their nominated representative. It also says the builder should give the extra cost and any extra time before the variation work starts, with an exception for urgent work needed to prevent danger or property damage, where the written variation may follow (NSW Government, contracts for residential building work; last updated 29 April 2026). The same page says a written contract is required where the contract price for residential building work is over $5,000 including GST. Whatever the state, a variation should be recorded with its price and its effect on time and coats, and approved in writing before the work is done.

instruction.heading: Colour approval and the cost of a change
instruction.body: Colour approval should be in writing, and it should identify the product, the colour code or the sample reference, the sheen, and the surfaces the colour applies to. A physical sample painted on a board in the room's light is better than a name on a card, because a colour can look different under other light. State that a colour change after the first coat can require more coats and extra cost, and record the client's acceptance of that before the new colour goes on. Where the client asks for a darker colour part-way through, that is a variation. Stop, record the request, give the client the price and the effect on coats and time, and obtain written approval before the new colour is applied. Keep the approved colour record with the job file so that the finish can be matched if touch-ups are needed later.

instruction.heading: Filing and the limits of this lesson
instruction.body: File the signed quote, each colour approval and each variation with the job record, and keep a note of the licence check. The records protect both the business and the client, and they show what was agreed if the job is later questioned. Completing this lesson does not give a painting licence, a certificate or any authority to quote for regulated building work.

procedure: Inspect the surfaces and record the scope, the preparation included, the paint system, and the number of coats for each surface.

Check the licence position for the job's value and state before the quote is issued (NSW: valued at more than $5,000 in labour and materials (including GST); WA: a licence is required for painting work valued at $1,000 or more; Victoria: painting-only jobs need no registration, but you must register with the BPC if you combine skills, such as plastering and painting; QLD, SA, TAS, ACT and NT: not confirmed by an official source).
State the exclusions in writing, including damp repairs, plaster defects, mould treatment, older-surface assessment and furniture moving.
Issue the quote with its validity date, and obtain the client's signed acceptance.
Obtain written colour approval with the product, the colour code or sample reference, and the sheen. Record the effect of any change after the first coat.
Record each variation with its price, its effect on time and coats, and the client's written approval before the work starts.
File the signed quote, colour approval, variation records and the licence check with the job record.

workedExamples.situation: Partway through a job, the client asks for a darker colour and says the first coat was fine.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the change be made without a new written approval?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. A colour change is a variation. A darker colour may need more coats, and it may need a different price. Stop, record the request, give the client the price and the effect on coats and time, and obtain written approval before applying the new colour. Keep the first colour and the new approval on the job record.

workedExamples.situation: While preparing an internal room for painting, you find a crack in the plaster that the quote did not include, and the client asks you to fill and paint over it.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can the filling be added as a casual extra?
workedExamples.reasoning: Treat it as a variation. Plaster defects were excluded from the quote, so filling and sanding them is outside the agreed scope. Describe the crack, photograph it with the client's permission, and give the client a written price and the effect on time. Do not fill or paint over the crack until the client has signed the variation. Explain that paint does not repair a crack, and that the filling is a separate item.

workedExamples.situation: A client has an internal painting job in New South Wales that comes to $4,800 in labour and materials, GST included. The same client has also asked for a new internal wall to be built as part of a wider renovation.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Does the painting quote need a licence check beyond the $4,800 figure?
workedExamples.reasoning: Yes. The painting figure alone is under $5000, but the NSW page says that stand-alone contracts for internal paintwork no longer need a licence “unless the paintwork is part of other home building work”. Whether the new wall is other home building work is not confirmed by an official source. The wall is part of the same renovation, so the scope of the whole renovation has to be checked before the quote is issued. Record the check, do not split the job to fall under a threshold, and confirm the position with the NSW regulator before quoting the combined work.

equipmentAndPpe: Quote template with fields for scope, surfaces, preparation, system, coats, exclusions, sheen, validity and approval
Colour samples, sample boards and product codes
Colour approval form with product, colour code, sheen and client signature
Variation form with description, price, effect on time and coats, and client approval
Measuring tape or laser measure for the room and surface schedule
Camera for condition photographs, used only with the client's permission
Licence check record showing the state, job value, date and page checked

commonErrors.error: Writing a quote that does not list the exclusions.
commonErrors.prevention: State the exclusions in writing, including damp repairs, plaster defects, mould treatment and older-surface assessment.

commonErrors.error: Changing the colour without written approval.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the variation, give the price and the effect on coats, and get written approval before painting.

commonErrors.error: Agreeing a variation by phone or in passing.
commonErrors.prevention: Put every variation in writing, with its price and its effect on time, and have it signed before the work is done.

commonErrors.error: Quoting a job without checking the licence position for its value and its scope.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the state threshold and the scope before the quote is issued, and record the check.

commonErrors.error: Splitting a job so that each part falls under a threshold.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the whole job, including any related building work, and confirm the position with the regulator.

commonErrors.error: Promising that paint will hide a defect that has not been repaired.
commonErrors.prevention: State the repair as an exclusion or a variation, and explain that paint does not repair cracks or damp.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: New South Wales: you need a contractor licence to do any residential building or trade work, including painting, which is valued at more than $5,000 in labour and materials (including GST) (NSW Government painting work page, last updated 23 June 2026). Since 2015, stand-alone contracts for internal paintwork no longer need a licence, unless the paintwork is part of other home building work. Quote the job value against the figure, and check the scope.

Queensland: the licence position for painting-only work is not confirmed by an official source. South Australia, Tasmania, the Australian Capital Territory and the Northern Territory: the licence position for painting is not confirmed by an official source.

Victoria: painting-only jobs need no registration. You must register with the BPC if you are using a combination of skills, such as plastering and painting, to complete a job (Consumer Victoria registration page, last updated 9 July 2025). Western Australia: painting work valued at $1,000 or more requires a licence, which is painting contractor registration (WA Government painters' scope of work page, last updated 23 December 2025).

Written variations and contracts for residential building work in New South Wales (last updated 29 April 2026): variations are in writing, signed by both parties, and the extra cost and time are given before the variation work starts, with an urgent-work exception. A written contract is required above $5,000 including GST.
Consumer guarantees for services (ACCC; last modified 28 August 2026): the due care and skill guarantee applies to services.
Completing this lesson does not give a painting or contractor licence, or authority to quote for regulated work.

qualityStandard: The quote states the scope, the surfaces, the preparation, the system, the coats, the exclusions, the colour approval route and the validity date.
Each variation and each colour change is recorded, priced and approved in writing before it is performed.
The licence threshold for the job's value and scope is checked, and the check is recorded before the quote is issued.
documentationEvidence: Signed quote with scope, surfaces, preparation, system, coats, exclusions and validity date.
Colour approval record with the product, colour code or sample reference, sheen and client signature.
Variation records, each with the description, the price, the effect on time and coats, and the client's written approval.
Licence check record with the state, the job value, the date, the page checked and the result.
summary: Quote the scope, the surfaces, the system, the coats and the exclusions in writing, so the client knows what the price covers.
Record and approve variations and colour changes in writing before the work is done, with their price and effect.
Check the state licence threshold and the scope before quoting, and record the check.

knowledgeChecks.question: During a job, the client asks for a darker colour. What should happen?
options: Record the request as a variation with its price and effect, and obtain written approval before painting
Change the colour because the client asked, and the crew will repaint the wall with the new colour
Use the new colour on one wall only without recording it, since the other walls can stay the same
Refuse without telling the client, since the change would take too long to make on the day

knowledgeChecks.question: What should a painting quote state in addition to the price?
options: Only the colour of the paint to be used
The scope, system, coats and exclusions
Nothing else is needed for the quote
Only the worker's name and the phone

knowledgeChecks.question: Which item belongs in the exclusions section of a painting quote?
options: The paint brand chosen by the client for the job
The number of coats to be applied on the wall
Damp repairs that are found during preparation

knowledgeChecks.question: What must happen before extra work on a variation is performed?
options: The extra price and the client's approval are recorded in writing
The worker chooses the price on the day, after the work has started
Nothing, if the client is happy with the work and the colour
